# How we make Critter act in real time

Turning Blender Studio’s Critter into an AI being that acts in real-time conversation.

Jul 18, 2026Pickle Team

PlayPause

0:00

en0:00

0:00

MuteUnmute

Enter fullscreen modeExit fullscreen mode

A personal AI becomes personal through context, and context grows through daily conversation. We believed people would speak more naturally, and more often, with a presence than with a tool: something alive you grow attached to, that remembers your life and eventually acts alongside you.

A presence needs more than a voice. It needs a body that acts in real-time conversation: moving with what it says, nodding along while you speak. Live avatars can already talk in real time. But below the face, nothing acts.

So we started with Critter, Blender Studio’s openly licensed 3D character ( [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)) from the open movie [Singularity](https://studio.blender.org/projects/singularity/): an expressive body with its own visual identity and rig. Critter, shown above, comes to life. Every glance, nod, and gesture, even the tail, is computed in real time as it speaks.

This post covers the body, the first piece we built: why we generate rig values instead of pixels, how a voice becomes a full body, and how we measure it.

## Why rig values instead of pixels

Live avatars today are usually built in one of two ways. A video diffusion model generates the pixels directly, or a neural twin (NeRF or 3D Gaussian splatting) re-renders a captured person.

Diffusion can produce any appearance and any motion, but it generates the character anew every frame, and the errors compound: the character drifts. Every diffusion stream also needs its own GPU, [roughly one H100 per 480p stream as of mid-2026](https://lemonslice.com/blog/lemonslice-2-1).

A NeRF/3DGS avatar is cheaper, though it still ties one GPU to each stream. Its renderer is learned from fine-tuning data, so production avatars stay inside talking-head reenactment, where data is dense. Move outside it — a larger turn, a shrug — and the render breaks down, because the data isn’t there.

![Comparison table of video diffusion, neural twins (NeRF, 3DGS), and rig plus generated motion: what each can perform live, what holds the form, what travels to the device (hundreds of numbers per frame for the rig), GPU per stream (~0.1 L40S for the rig), and what the body can be](https://pickle.com/whitepaper/a_table_desktop.png)Three ways to build a live body, against what conversation requires.

A rig (the skeleton and expression controls inside every game character) has neither problem. Its shape lives in the asset, in geometry and skinning, so the character never drifts: the same body, every frame. The pixels are drawn on the viewer’s device by fixed, well-defined rules, so the frame never collapses. And because rendering happens on the device, resolution costs the server nothing: the same stream of values draws Critter at 480p or 4K.

What a rig needs is the motion.

Form is the one choice left. Photorealistic bodies pay the uncanny-valley tax: the closer to human, the harsher a small error reads. A stylized creature escapes it, and it is honest. The being is an AI, and the form says so. The price is data: no motion-capture dataset contains a body with these ears and this tail.

## How a voice becomes a full body

### Two models and one designed layer

![Architecture diagram: character voice audio feeds the Face Model (NVIDIA Audio2Face-3D, 68 expression channels at 60 fps) and the Head Motion Model (6 head-pose channels); the Motion Synthesis Layer retargets the face and turns the six head-pose values into a body, emitting 257 rig control channels at 60 fps for rendering](https://pickle.com/whitepaper/b_architecture_desktop.png)

The system is two learned models and one layer we designed. Audio drives a facial model (NVIDIA’s Audio2Face-3D, 68 blendshape weights at 60 fps) and a pose model (six channels: the head’s rotations and translations). The synthesis layer retargets the face onto the rig and turns those six numbers into everything below the head. Each frame out is 257 control values — the full set we drive on Critter’s rig, brow to tail tip. The learned models run on a GPU; the synthesis layer is arithmetic on a CPU; the user’s device renders the values.

### Answering before you stop speaking

To feel conversational, the reply has to land fast. [Human turn-taking gaps center around 200 ms](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2705608/); past half a second, silence starts to read as hesitation. Our budget is 500 ms.

To get under it, the response is inferred before you stop speaking. While you are still talking, the LLM drafts a reply and our models infer its motion. If you keep talking, the draft is discarded and the agent keeps listening. If you stop, the pre-generated response and its motion are sent and rendered.

![Preemptive inference timeline: while the user is still speaking the turn decision, LLM draft, TTS, and Audio2Motion run ahead with a 0.2s onset buffer, so the first audible voice lands about 0.5 seconds after the turn ends; preemptive timing shown assumes ideal conditions](https://pickle.com/whitepaper/c_streaming_desktop.png)

### Six numbers become a body

Below the head, the data runs out. Head motion transfers from human video because a nod is a nod on any skeleton. Body motion does not transfer: co-speech gesture models are trained on human skeletons, and nothing in that data knows what these ears and this tail should do. So rather than generate the body, we derive it.

We drive body motion from the head pose, through a physics layer built for Critter’s body. The head pose carries the rhythm and the emotion of the voice; the body follows with delay, inertia, and weight. The layer is pure computation, zero learned weights.

The head-motion model is trained on videos of humans talking, so its strongest rotations peak at 6.5 to 8 degrees. On a creature that is meant to act, that reads as stillness. We amplify the rotations 3.5x, large enough to read as acting. Each part then follows with its own delay: the chest first, the tail last, with inertia carried down the bone chain.

The bar comes from Critter’s own film. In animation, the attack of a move is its fast opening stretch, the part where the motion commits. Across roughly 100 head moves in the film, an attack takes about 0.2 seconds, and its middle two frames carry half the distance. That is the timing signature we tune toward.

We tune the layer in an agentic loop. Every parameter change must pass automated checks against those measurements, and then a person watches the motion and picks the better one. That eye is the only place taste enters the system.

## How we evaluate

### Preference study

The same agent, the same voice, and the same ten conversations ran once through our rig and once through a state-of-the-art real-time video diffusion avatar. The diffusion side used its official integration at default settings and animated the same character from a reference image. Twenty-five raters watched the ten paired conversations blind and picked the one that felt more alive and natural, or neither.

Raters chose the rig in 86.8% of the 250 judgments, the diffusion stream in 10.8%, and neither in 2.4%.

![Liveness preference bar chart: rig (ours) 86.8%, neither 2.4%, video diffusion 10.8% — n = 250 judgements, 25 raters × 10 conversations, error bar = 95% CI of the rig share](https://pickle.com/whitepaper/d_preference_desktop.png)

One caveat we want on the record: real-time diffusion avatars are tuned for human faces, and animating a stylized creature from a single reference image is not their best case. It is, however, the deployment case. To put this character live today, these are the two available paths, and the study compares them as they ship.

### Latency and cost

We measure from the end of your turn to the first visible reaction. The rig moved at +400 ms; the diffusion stream at +800 ms. Agent and voice were identical, so the gap is the avatar layer.

On cost, as of July 2026: diffusion streams sell for $0.16 to $0.22 a minute, and managed avatar streams list between $0.10 and $0.37. Ours runs on a tenth of an L40S per stream at 60 fps — about $0.003 a minute of GPU at AWS list prices. That is our raw compute against their retail pricing, not a margin-for-margin comparison, but the two-orders-of-magnitude gap is the architecture.

![Latency and cost charts: rig (ours) reacts at +400 ms versus +800 ms for video diffusion; on a log cost scale the rig runs at about $0.003 a minute of raw GPU versus $0.16–0.22 listed for video diffusion and $0.10–0.37 for managed avatar streams](https://pickle.com/whitepaper/e_latencycost_desktop.png)

## Limitations and what’s next

Today the body hears only its own voice. You arrive as turn events: Critter knows that you are speaking, not how. And it does not know what its words mean. It cannot say “come here” while making a come-here gesture, nod when it agrees, or shake its head when it disagrees.

The next input is the user’s stream. We are validating a causal diffusion model that maps your voice and movement to the avatar’s listening motion, and feeds it into the same channel we use today. In the coming months, Critter will react to how you speak.

Ultimately the body should follow the context of the conversation. Autoregressive diffusion models already turn text into motion in real time. We believe the context understanding belongs in the LLM, to leverage its scale. The LLM will direct the body just by calling a tool, in real time.
